analysis.one_liner: Funds homeless services with new taxes on luxury property sales, anonymous buyers, and mega-landlords.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 16, 2025 with 30 cosponsors, all Democrats, the bill was sent to five House committees and none has scheduled a hearing or vote on it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would pour roughly $27 billion a year into homelessness programs: grants to cities that stop arresting people for sleeping outside, a new block grant to build housing affordable to the poorest households, bigger emergency shelter and housing funds, library pilot programs for homeless people, and help with voting for people without fixed addresses. It pays for much of this with three new federal taxes: a 5% tax on sales of property worth $10 million or more, a 10% tax on property deals involving anonymous shell companies, and a 1% tax on the rent charged by landlords who own more than 1,000 units in one metro area, 2,000 units total, or 500 units spread across three or more states. Landlords can avoid the rental tax by accepting rent stabilization, just-cause eviction rules, or bans on rejecting tenants with housing vouchers.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are homeless or housing-unstable: they would get permanent affordable housing, shelter beds, street outreach, legal aid, bathrooms and other basic infrastructure, mobile crisis teams instead of police responses, and help protecting their belongings and voting. Cities and nonprofit providers get the funding to do this, with grants weighted toward places that stop penalizing homelessness and prioritize people of color, veterans, people with disabilities, LGBTQ people, and others hit hardest.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $100 million a year for ten years for states and cities to create alternatives to criminalizing homelessness, including pre-arrest diversion programs and mobile crisis teams of health workers instead of police [S2].

Creates a CDBG Plus block grant (up to $6 billion a year, topped up by the new tax revenue) reserved for homeless, housing-unstable, and cost-burdened households, and specifically allows building housing permanently affordable to people earning 30% or less of area median income, plus public bathrooms, water fountains, and places to rest [S2].

Authorizes $10 billion a year each for the Emergency Solutions Grant and Continuum of Care programs (minus tax revenue credited to them) and $1 billion a year for FEMA emergency food and shelter grants, including shelter conversions and tiny homes [S2].

Conditions federal homelessness funding on localities not enforcing laws that punish people for sleeping outside, giving notice before clearing encampments and safeguarding personal property for at least 30 days, having voting-access plans for people without addresses, and adopting non-discrimination policies [S2].

Grants library systems $10 million a year for programs serving homeless patrons, makes it far easier for homeless-service providers to obtain vacant federal buildings, and permanently authorizes the U.S. Interagency Council on Homelessness with an advisory board made up mostly of people who have experienced homelessness [S2].

Directs the Election Assistance Commission to study and fund ways to help homeless and housing-unstable people vote, including addressing ID requirements and the effects of laws that penalize homelessness [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers and buyers of homes and buildings worth $10 million or more (splitting a 5% transfer tax), shell companies and trusts whose real owners are hidden from public records (10% on property deals), and large corporate landlords, who pay 1% of rent unless their units fall under rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protection laws. Any spending not covered by the new taxes would come from the Treasury.
analysis.who_pays_short: Luxury property sellers, anonymous buyers, giant landlords

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $27 billion a year in new spending; the new taxes are credited toward those totals, but the authorizations are sized as the shortfall after tax revenue, so any gap is absorbed by the Treasury and the federal deficit [S2].

The 1% rental tax applies only in places without rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protections, which could give big landlords a reason to lobby against tenant protections or pass the tax to renters in unregulated markets [S2].

Tying federal funds to requirements that localities stop enforcing camping bans and meet detailed policy conditions would strike many mayors as federal overreach, and some jurisdictions could simply decline the money [S2].

A 5% tax on high-end property transfers, shared between buyer and seller, would modestly increase the cost of large real estate transactions and could slightly reduce them; the anonymous-entity tax creates a compliance burden for legitimate structures unless entities join the public legal-identifier registry [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete for a visible and growing population—people sleeping outside, in cars, and in shelters—and the costs fall on a narrow slice of the property market: $10 million-plus sales, hidden ownership, and landlords with portfolios of 1,000 units or more. The main honest objections are fiscal (the taxes may not fully cover the authorizations) and the risk that the rental tax nudges big landlords toward raising rents where no tenant protections exist. The design also locks homelessness funding to speculative-property revenue, which could swing with the real estate market.

outcome.mechanism: The bill has sat with five House committees since its July 2025 introduction, and none has taken it up.

narrative.text: Rep. Pramila Jayapal introduced the bill in the House on July 16, 2025 [S4].

The same day, it was referred to the Financial Services, House Administration, Judiciary, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees, with the Speaker to decide which gets lead jurisdiction [S4].
The bill has 30 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support [S3].
No committee has scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote, and the action history shows nothing beyond the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homelessness programs continue at current funding levels, and luxury property sellers, anonymous property buyers, and large corporate landlords avoid the new taxes the bill would impose on them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large landlords and luxury sellers avoid the taxes

for.name: Rep. Pramila Jayapal

sides.party_line_note: All 31 supporters—the sponsor and 30 cosponsors—are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on [S3].

industries.note: They would pay 1% of rent collected unless their units come under rent control, just-cause eviction, or source-of-income protection laws—an unusual design that rewards landlords for accepting tenant protections tenants themselves want. In unregulated markets, the tax could be passed through to renters.
A 5% tax split between buyer and seller would raise the cost of high-end property sales, where ownership is concentrated among the wealthiest households and investors.

industries.industry: Anonymous property owners and shell companies
industries.note: A 10% tax on property transfers involving entities whose beneficial owners are not in public records would push hidden ownership into the open or make it expensive, reducing money laundering and all-cash investor competition for homes.
They would administer most of the new grant funding for shelter, diversion programs, crisis teams, and legal aid, expanding their role and revenue.
Libraries, which already serve as de facto daytime shelters, would receive pilot grants to run programs for homeless patrons.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to five committees rarely advance; with no Republican cosponsors, no scheduled hearings, and no committee action months into the two-year session, this bill is very unlikely to reach a House floor vote in the 119th Congress.
